Cannabis 101

How to Use Cannabis Discreetly (and Legally) in Michigan

Edibles, vapes, drinks, capsules and topicals compared for smell, timing and dose control, plus where Michigan law lets you use cannabis.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20266 min read

06min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. Discreet cannabis use starts with Michigan law
  2. Edibles: low odor, slow start
  3. Vapes: no smoke, less lingering smell
  4. Capsules and tablets: measured doses
  5. Drinks, powders and drink mixes
  6. Concentrates you can eat
  7. Topicals and transdermal patches
  8. Choosing a method: onset, duration, odor and dose control
  9. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • In Michigan, discretion means privacy and courtesy: public use is not allowed, and property owners can ban it.
  • Edibles, capsules, drinks and topicals give off little smell, but anything you swallow is slow to start.
  • Vapes skip smoke and ash, yet the vapor still smells like cannabis.
  • Choose a method by onset, duration, odor and how precisely you can measure a dose.

Discreet cannabis use is about privacy and courtesy, not dodging the rules. In Michigan, adults 21 and older can use cannabis on private property where it's allowed, but not in public. Within those lines, plenty of discreet ways to consume cannabis are smoke-free or low in odor, from edibles and drinks to capsules and topicals. Here's how each compares on smell, timing and dose control.

Discreet cannabis use starts with Michigan law

People choose low-key formats for many reasons, from roommates to visiting family. The law sets the boundaries:

  • No public use. Michigan's adult-use law doesn't allow consuming cannabis in a public place.
  • The property decides. Whoever owns or manages a property can ban smoking or use there. If you rent, your landlord can ban or limit cannabis, but a lease can't forbid you from lawfully possessing it and consuming it by means other than smoking.
  • Not in vehicles. No one may use cannabis while driving or operating a boat, snowmobile, off-road vehicle or aircraft, and smoking in a car's passenger area on a public road isn't allowed.

Discretion never stretches those lines. Our Michigan cannabis law guide covers the details.

Edibles: low odor, slow start

Discreet edibles such as a sealed gummy or chocolate give off little smell, and there's nothing to light. The trade-off is time. Swallowed cannabis passes through your digestive system first. Health Canada says you might feel the first effects 30 minutes to 2 hours after eating, that full effects can take up to 4 hours and that effects may last as long as 12 hours.

In Michigan, an adult-use edible serving holds no more than 10 mg of THC, and a package tops out at 200 mg. Start with a small piece, wait and keep edibles in their child-resistant packaging. Our guide to what edibles are covers the basics.

Homemade edibles

Baking your own lets you choose the flavor and the portion size, but a home batch is harder to measure. If you'd like to try, start with our cannabutter recipe, cut small portions and label everything clearly.

Vapes: no smoke, less lingering smell

A vaporizer heats cannabis without burning it, so there's no smoke, ash or lighter. People often say the scent fades sooner than smoke does, though there's little research on that, and vapor still carries the aroma of the plant's terpenes. Effects arrive within seconds to minutes, which makes it easy to take a little, pause and decide. Keep the device in a closed case, away from kids and pets.

Capsules and tablets: measured doses

Capsules have little to no smell and come in fixed doses, so they're among the most predictable formats. In Michigan, an adult-use capsule dose is capped at 10 mg of THC. Like edibles, they're swallowed, so they start slowly and last a long time. Take one, then wait.

Drinks, powders and drink mixes

Poured into a glass, a THC seltzer, or one of the cannabis drink mixes you stir into lemonade, looks like any other drink. That's discreet, but it also means an open drink should stay with you, out of reach of kids and guests. In Michigan, beverages hold no more than 10 mg of THC per serving and 100 mg per container. Some makers say their drinks start faster, but plan as if each one is as slow as an edible. Our comparison of THC drinks and edibles explains the timing.

Concentrates you can eat

Some concentrates, such as distillate and RSO, can be swallowed or mixed into food. They're far stronger than flower: in Washington State's legal market from 2014 to 2016, extracts averaged about 69% THC, more than three times the average for flower. A tiny portion goes a long way, so measure carefully and mix thoroughly. Concentrates are best left to experienced consumers.

Topicals and transdermal patches

Lotions, balms and salves are rubbed into the skin, with no smoke and nothing to swallow. Transdermal patches are different: they're designed to pass cannabinoids through the skin to reach your bloodstream over time. Michigan allows up to 100 mg of THC per dose in products that aren't taken by mouth, such as patches, compared with 10 mg in an adult-use edible serving. Read the label closely, and see our guide to cannabis topicals.

Choosing a method: onset, duration, odor and dose control

MethodOnsetHow long it lastsOdorDose control
VapeSeconds to minutesHours; some effects up to about 6Noticeable up closePuff by puff
Edibles30 minutes to 2 hours; full effect up to 4 hoursUp to 12 hoursVery lowFixed mg per piece
CapsulesSlow, like ediblesLong, like ediblesVery lowFixed mg per capsule
DrinksPlan on edible timingPlan on edible timingVery lowmg per serving
Eaten concentratesSlow, like ediblesLong, like ediblesLowHard; very potent
Topicals and patchesVaries by productVaries by productLowRead the label

If you want predictability, fixed-dose capsules and edibles help. If you want smokeless cannabis with short, adjustable sessions at home, a vape lets you go one puff at a time. Whatever you choose, start low and give it time.

Our budtenders are happy to walk you through each format, or you can browse your store's menu in our online shop. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

What is the least smelly way to use cannabis?

Formats you swallow or apply. Edibles, capsules, drinks and topicals give off little or no smell once they're out of the package. Vapes skip smoke, but the vapor still smells like cannabis. Airtight, child-resistant containers keep the aroma in, and store them where children and pets can't get to them.

Is it legal to use cannabis in public in Michigan?

No. Michigan's adult-use law doesn't allow consuming cannabis in a public place, and whoever owns a property can ban it there. You also can't use it while driving or operating a boat or snowmobile, and smoking in a car's passenger area on a public road isn't allowed. Use it on private property where it's permitted.

How long do edibles take compared with vapes?

Inhaled cannabis is felt within seconds to minutes, with full effects within about 30 minutes. With edibles, first effects show up between half an hour and two hours after eating, and the full effect can take up to 4 hours. That's why the usual advice is to wait before taking more of an edible.

Do cannabis drinks act faster than edibles?

Sometimes, but plan as if they don't. Some drinks are made to come on sooner, yet you still swallow them, so your body processes them much like an edible. Sip one serving, give it time and don't stack a second drink on top. A Michigan THC drink holds up to 10 mg of THC per serving.

  3. Health Canada: Cannabis, lower your riskscanada.ca
  4. Health Canada: New cannabis products, what Canadians need to know (video transcript)canada.ca

  6. Smart R. et al., Variation in cannabis potency and prices in a newly legal market: evidence from 30 million cannabis sales in Washington state, Addiction (2017)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
